tldr: We audited a "robotic world model" (learned simulator) that lets a quadruped robot learn to walk inside a neural network, rebuilding it from scratch without a GPU on a 2017 everyday laptop. The results expose harsh realities: optimizing for one-step accuracy actually degrades long-term rollouts, and lower simulator prediction error does not translate into learning a walking policy.
overview:
In reinforcement learning for legged robots, "learned simulators" (world models)—where neural networks replace traditional physics engines by mimicking the robot's dynamics entirely—have gained major attention. In particular, the prominent Robotic World Model (RWM) and its uncertainty-aware extension, RWM-U, have claimed that robots can learn behaviors from real or simulated data and acquire walking policies entirely inside their own imagination.

Yet when robotics researchers try to put these world models to work, practical questions quickly emerge: Does the published training recipe actually help long-term rollouts? Does the reported uncertainty represent true error? How can we tell a good simulator from a bad one before running it on a robot? Taking an independent third-party stance, this study audits and replicates the released RWM code and checkpoints end-to-end, running mostly on a 2017 dual-core laptop without a GPU.

The audit confirmed RWM's central claim that multi-step rollout training is vital for long-term prediction. However, standard one-step-ahead evaluations misjudge design choices completely. More critically, even simulators fine-tuned on physical data to improve prediction accuracy yielded policies that fell over, uncovering a stark disconnect between model accuracy and walking skill.
contributions: Built an exact from-scratch re-implementation of RWM matching the released code, losses, and gradients, while uncovering two implementation flaws—including a one-control-step command delay in the released pipeline—and measuring their impact.
Validated that training on self-rollouts vastly outperforms one-step training over long horizons, while showing via Lyapunov exponents why one-step evaluations reverse this ranking.
Proved that while RWM-U's uncertainty ranks errors reliably, individual variance heads collapse to zero due to loss formulation flaws, severely under-sizing absolute errors.
Trained walking policies inside 33 simulator variants and tested them in a hand-built MuJoCo physics model, demonstrating that open-loop prediction accuracy fails entirely to predict walking success.
Documented nine of the authors' own claims that were later withdrawn, along with what caught them, highlighting the critical role of pre-registration and reproducibility in robot learning.

sections.heading: Why audit a world model on a 2017 laptop?
sections.summary: Legged robot controllers are increasingly trained inside learned simulators, yet their evaluation often leans on one-step prediction accuracy. Without using any GPU, this study trained and evaluated over 100 simulators on a low-spec laptop to rigorously audit existing claims and practical questions from end to end.
sections.details:
Walking policies for legged robots are typically trained via reinforcement learning in physics simulators and then transferred to real hardware (Sim-to-Real). In contrast, learned simulators (world models) train neural networks to predict next states from past histories and joint commands, letting policies learn entirely inside imagined trajectories. Robotic World Model (RWM) on the ANYmal D quadruped, along with its follow-up RWM-U that penalizes ensemble uncertainty to keep policies safe, are prime examples of this paradigm.

However, when executing a learned simulator, the model recursively feeds its own past predictions back as future inputs (rollouts). While training a policy requires unrolling for 100 steps (2 seconds at 50 Hz) or more, many papers and architectural choices are justified solely through one-step-ahead accuracy. This fails to evaluate how small errors compound over time.

To investigate, the authors acted as independent auditors using an ordinary 2017 Intel Core i5 laptop (2 cores, 8 GiB RAM) without a GPU. After resolving discrepancies between code and paper, they confirmed bit-exact parity with the released implementation, auditing 101 recurrent simulators, 200 compressed copies, and evaluating policy performance in a hand-crafted MuJoCo model.

sections.heading: World models, compounding errors, and pitfalls in prior work
sections.summary: The primary obstacle in recurrent simulators is compounding error, where discrepancies grow exponentially over time. This section surveys multi-step rollout training, ensemble uncertainty estimation, and dynamical stability analysis to establish the audit's scope.
sections.details:
A fundamental vulnerability of world models in robotics is compounding error arising from autoregressive rollouts. Mitigations include multi-step training—unrolling predicted trajectories for several steps before backpropagating—and truncating rollout horizons. Conversely, teacher forcing, which constantly feeds ground-truth states, achieves high one-step accuracy but suffers from objective mismatch, failing over long horizons.

In offline reinforcement learning, subtracting ensemble disagreement from rewards is standard practice to prevent policies from exploiting out-of-distribution dynamics. However, multi-head ensembles sharing a single trunk risk underestimating disagreement, and non-likelihood losses can cause variance predictions to collapse.

To audit these claims on unseen data and policy training, this work leverages tools like finite-time Lyapunov exponents (FTLE) to evaluate recurrent network stability and kinematic residuals to test the physical consistency between predicted velocities and positions.

sections.heading: Behind the scenes: ANYmal D, the dataset, and strict measurement rules
sections.summary: The test platform is ANYmal D, a 12-joint quadruped. Analyzing the 200-second public log revealed clean, simulator-derived trajectories devoid of falls, prompting a rigorous evaluation framework based on strictly independent trials.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Target Robot and State Space
The target platform is ANYmal D, featuring 3 degrees of freedom per leg (hip abduction, hip flexion, knee) totaling 12 joints. The simulator state vector comprises 45 dimensions: base linear velocity (3), base angular velocity (3), projected gravity (3), along with joint positions (12), velocities (12), and torques (12). Joint position commands are issued at 50 Hz (20 ms intervals).

### 3.2 Reality of the Released Dataset
The public dataset consisted of a single file containing 10,000 rows (200 seconds). Analysis revealed distinct traits:
- It concatenates ten 20-second episodes, with joint velocities and commands resetting to exactly zero every 10 rows. Because exact zero resets cannot occur on hardware, the data clearly originates from simulation.
- No falls exist anywhere in the dataset; thighs touch the ground in only a single timestep out of 10,000.
- All motion is trotting at a fixed cadence of 27 steps (~0.54 s cycle), with commands switching only once mid-episode across 21 discrete velocity settings.
- Commanded positions lead actual positions by 4 steps (80 ms), reflecting an actuator with delayed position tracking.

### 3.3 Simulator Architecture and Training
The network uses a 2-layer GRU (hidden size 256) reading a 32-step history to predict the mean and variance of next-state deltas. The single model has ~1.42M parameters, while the 5-head ensemble contains ~2.0M. Models were trained for 2,500 iterations using Adam, matching the original setup.

### 3.4 Independent Units and Evaluation Metrics
Evaluating on overlapping windows artificially inflates statistical confidence. Here, non-overlapping 368-step trajectories extracted from held-out episodes (yielding only 2 independent windows per episode) served as strict independent units. Metrics include normalized mean absolute error $E(h)$, scaled by state standard deviations, and retained skill $K(h)$, which measures improvement over a baseline that simply holds the last known state.

sections.heading: Rebuilding the model and finding two bugs in the release pipeline
sections.summary: Cross-checking the paper against the code allowed an exact re-implementation matching outputs, losses, and gradients. This process exposed discrepancies with the written paper and uncovered a critical flaw: joint commands fed into the model with a one-step delay.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Bit-Exact Matching Before Training
Before training new models, the authors verified that their re-implementation matched the public checkpoint's forward passes, loss components, and backward gradients bit for bit. This guaranteed that any performance differences down the line stemmed from training methodology or data rather than wiring bugs.

### 4.2 Discrepancies Between Paper and Code
Inspecting the code revealed several gaps relative to the manuscript:
- Loss components: The paper described 2 loss terms, but the codebase contained 7 terms, with 3 disabled via configuration files.
- Termination and contact networks: Sub-networks predicting foot contacts and episode termination were trained solely one step ahead on ground-truth states, never receiving rollout training.
- Missing discount factor: The rollout discount factor mentioned in the paper was absent from the code.
- Uncertainty definition: While the paper formulated uncertainty as ensemble variance, the code computed standard deviation (confirmed with the authors as intentional).

### 4.3 Two Pipeline Flaws
The release evaluation pipeline contained two notable bugs:
- Ignored episode boundaries: Because termination flags were set to zero everywhere, 352 invalid training windows (3.5%) crossed episode boundaries, splicing the tail of one run into the start of another.
- One-step command delay: While training paired state $t$ with command $t$, the public evaluation script mistakenly fed commands from step $t-1$. Correcting this alignment worsened the public checkpoint's one-step prediction error by 55%. This timing mismatch was invisible on standard trajectory plots and only came to light by questioning physical unit conventions.

sections.heading: Self-rollout training wins, but one-step checks completely flip the verdict
sections.summary: RWM's core claim—that training on self-rollouts beats one-step training over long horizons—replicated decisively on held-out episodes. Shockingly, evaluating strictly one step ahead favored teacher forcing, reversing the outcome and misjudging model utility.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Verification on Held-Out Episodes: Rollout Training Dominates
Using a 5-fold cross-validation setup holding out 2 episodes per fold, models were evaluated across 20 independent unseen trajectories. At 368 steps ahead (~7.4 s), models trained on self-rollouts achieved 5.9 times lower relative L1 error compared to teacher forcing across all 10 held-out episodes without exception (Figure F2).

### 5.2 One-Step Checks Misjudge Performance
However, when evaluating the very same models one step ahead, teacher-forced models scored better. Relying solely on one-step accuracy would falsely indicate that teacher forcing is superior. In reality, errors in teacher-forced rollouts compound so rapidly that by step 29 (~0.6 s), their predictions perform worse than a naive floor baseline that simply freezes the last observed state.

In physical terms, after 2 seconds (100 steps), the teacher-forced model drifted by 7.0 degrees per joint and lost track of robot position by 0.84 m, whereas the rollout-trained model held errors to 3.4 degrees and 0.51 m.

### 5.3 Why Rankings Reverse: Error Growth vs. Contraction
This reversal was analyzed using the maximum finite-time Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_1$, which measures whether a simulator amplifies or attenuates small state perturbations. Training rollout horizon strongly correlated with $\lambda_1$ (correlation −0.97). Models trained only 1 to 2 steps ahead amplified errors exponentially ($\lambda_1 > 0$), while those trained with rollouts of 8 steps or more learned contracting dynamics ($\lambda_1 < 0$). Teacher forcing never exposes the network to its own erroneous outputs, leaving it brittle during autonomous rollouts.

captions.F2: Figure F2: Difference in relative L1 error at 368 steps between teacher-forcing and self-rollout training. Red markers denote held-out evaluation episodes; all lie comfortably above zero, confirming rollout training's decisive advantage.

sections.heading: Uncertainty estimates: rankings hold up, but scales are broken
sections.summary: RWM-U's ensemble disagreement accurately ranked the relative severity of errors. However, the absolute magnitude was severely underestimated, and individual prediction variances collapsed to near-zero due to a flawed loss formulation.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Two Flavors of Uncertainty
The codebase computes two distinct uncertainty metrics: the variance predicted by each network head (aleatoric noise) and the spread among the 5 ensemble heads (epistemic uncertainty). Only the ensemble spread was used as a reward penalty for policy training.

### 6.2 Variance Collapse in Individual Heads
The variance predicted by individual heads steadily shrank during training, effectively collapsing to zero (Figure F5). This stemmed from the loss function: rather than negative log-likelihood, the code minimized the mean squared error of samples drawn from the predicted distribution. The expected loss evaluates to $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}] = (\hat{\mu} - y)^2 + \sigma^2$, which reaches its global minimum when $\sigma = 0$. With no logarithmic penalty to push back, Adam drove $\sigma$ downward at each iteration, resulting in predicted standard deviations 1,827 times smaller than actual one-step errors (Figure F6).

### 6.3 Ensemble Spread: Good Rankings, Broken Calibration
In contrast, the spread across the 5 ensemble heads tracked true rollout error well, achieving a Spearman rank correlation of +0.90 at 100 steps. It reliably indicates which states are comparatively more dangerous.

Nonetheless, its absolute scale was miscalibrated. While a properly calibrated Gaussian places ~68% of residuals within $\pm 1\sigma$, the ensemble spread covered only 4.6% of outcomes. To encompass true rollout errors, the spread had to be scaled up by $31\times$ at 100 steps and $42\times$ at 368 steps (Figure F7). Sharing 89% of parameters across a common GRU trunk and feeding back the ensemble mean rather than individual trajectories fueled this extreme overconfidence.

captions.F5: Figure F5: Collapse of predicted standard deviation $\sigma$ during training. (a) Under the implemented loss (blue), both bounds decay monotonically, whereas a proper log-likelihood loss (green) recovers. (b) The rate of collapse matches Adam's step size.
captions.F6: Figure F6: Overconfidence in predicted standard deviation across heads. The implemented model (blue) and public checkpoint (purple) underestimate true error by several orders of magnitude compared to the likelihood-corrected model (green).
captions.F7: Figure F7: Ratio of true error to predicted spread over rollout horizons. Overconfidence worsens over time in the public checkpoint (solid purple), but unrolling each head independently (dashed) significantly mitigates the issue.

sections.heading: How should a simulator be screened before training a policy?
sections.summary: We evaluated future-free metrics like Lyapunov exponents and kinematic residuals to assess simulator quality without recorded test trajectories. While useful for initial filtering, they cannot substitute for multi-step rollout errors and failed to act as online runtime monitors.
sections.details:
### 7.1 Comparing Four Screening Metrics
To evaluate simulators prior to reinforcement learning, four metrics were tested:
- Ground-truth dependent: 1-step error $E_1$, 8-step error $E_8$
- Future-free: Maximum finite-time Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_1$ (error growth rate), kinematic residual $\bar{r}_J$ (discrepancy between integrated joint velocity and predicted joint angle)

### 7.2 Benchmark Outcomes and Pitfalls
Evaluating 57 recurrent models revealed that one-step error $E_1$ correlated negatively with 100-step rollout error (−0.50), reaffirming that lower one-step error often indicates worse multi-step rollouts.

Among future-free checks, kinematic residual $\bar{r}_J$ correlated strongly (0.95) under logged commands, but dropped to 0.83 under dynamic policy actions. Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_1$ succeeded at filtering out fragile one-step-trained models, but failed to register the accuracy degradation caused by weight pruning.

### 7.3 Failure of Runtime Alarms
Attempts to build runtime alarms that detect when a simulator goes off the rails during rollouts proved unsuccessful. Physical plausibility does not guarantee state accuracy: a simulator can easily predict physically consistent, dynamically self-contained configurations that are completely wrong.

sections.heading: Compression for on-robot deployment: pruning traps and CPU speed
sections.summary: To assess viability on edge hardware, models were subjected to dynamic quantization and weight pruning. While pruning 30% of weights retained 90% of skill one step ahead, performance plummeted below naive baselines after two seconds, exposing horizon-dependent compression limits.
sections.details:
### 8.1 Compression vs. Rollout Horizon
Deploying simulators on real robots requires minimizing memory and latency. Models were tested using dynamic 8-bit integer quantization and unstructured pruning (zeroing lowest-magnitude weights), evaluating retained skill $K(h)$ across rollout steps.

Quantization performed robustly, retaining 95.2% of skill even at 368 steps. Pruning 30% of weights maintained 90% skill one step ahead, but retained skill collapsed to 39% after 2 seconds (100 steps) and fell below the naive zero-prediction floor at 7.4 seconds. Relying on one-step tests to validate pruning masks catastrophic long-term failure.

### 8.2 Recovery via Brief Fine-Tuning
This lost skill was fully restored: 500 fine-tuning iterations with masked weights brought performance to 102.2% of the unpruned baseline. Similarly, narrowing GRU hidden width from 256 to 192 followed by fine-tuning preserved ~90% of skill.

### 8.3 CPU Benchmarks on a 2017 Laptop
Even on older CPUs lacking VNNI instructions, compiling with TorchScript and applying 8-bit quantization cut inference latency to 0.75× baseline. Against a 20 ms control budget, even the heaviest 5-head ensemble executed single-threaded inference in under 4 ms per step, running comfortably faster than real time.

sections.heading: Robot-level verdict: when more accurate simulators destroy walking
sections.summary: Policies trained inside various world models were tested in a hand-crafted MuJoCo physics simulation. In a striking reversal, simulators fine-tuned on physical data to improve prediction accuracy produced policies that failed to walk entirely.
sections.details:
### 9.1 Hand-Built MuJoCo Environment
Lacking GPUs to run the original Isaac Lab environment, ANYmal D dynamics were built by hand in MuJoCo 3.10 from public hardware specs. Replacing the proprietary actuator network with a fitted delayed position controller allowed the public policy to complete 79 of 80 episodes, matching real-world tracking metrics.

### 9.2 Complete Failure of From-Scratch Simulators
Policies trained inside simulators learned from scratch on the released dataset fell immediately in physics tests. Because the training data contained zero falls, simulators could not imagine falling dynamics. Policies quickly learned to exploit these blind spots to accumulate imaginary rewards (model exploitation).

### 9.3 6 Million Physical Transitions Still Fail to Yield Walking
To resolve data scarcity, a diverse dataset of 6 million transitions was generated from MuJoCo to train a new world model from scratch. This model surpassed the public checkpoint in prediction accuracy at 1, 8, and 100 steps. Yet policies trained within it chose immediate self-termination on step 1, scoring 0.000 for walking. The ensemble disagreement penalty was so punishing that policies opted to end episodes immediately rather than risk taking steps.

### 9.4 The Adaptation Ladder: Fine-Tuning Induces Failure
The most striking finding came from fine-tuning the public checkpoint on MuJoCo transitions. Just 20 steps of fine-tuning improved 1-step and 8-step prediction accuracy, yet entirely broke the model's ability to yield walking policies. Open-loop error reduction directly conflicted with policy viability. Only a closed-loop check—evaluating how well a known walking policy tracked commands inside the simulator—accurately ranked simulator viability.

sections.heading: Nine mistakes we made and the guardrails that caught them
sections.summary: The authors openly catalog nine false conclusions they initially believed during the project before retracting them. A claims ledger, pre-registered test criteria, and parity checks against released code provided the guardrails needed to avoid self-deception.
sections.details:
### 10.1 Nine Retracted Claims
The paper lists nine claims initially accepted by the authors but later retracted upon deeper inspection. Notable examples include:
- Significant separation from teacher forcing at step 8: Early statistical significance vanished once overlapping windows were eliminated in favor of strictly independent trajectories, leaving the result unsettled under pre-registered criteria.
- Fixing variance heads would improve overall accuracy: Adopting a proper likelihood loss stopped variance collapse, but the predicted uncertainty became input-invariant, rendering it ineffective as an adaptive estimator.
- Selecting simulators via one-step error: Initial small-scale experiments suggested one-step and multi-step errors aligned, but testing a wider pool revealed the relationship completely inverted.

### 10.2 Tools That Caught the Errors
Structured research protocols were essential in catching these missteps:
- Claims Ledger: Every assertion was assigned a unique ID; refuted claims were updated with explicit superseding entries rather than erased.
- Pre-registration: Evaluation criteria and statistical thresholds were committed before analyzing data, forcing null outcomes to be reported as "not settled."
- Differential Testing: Running released checkpoints through the rebuilt pipeline directly exposed the one-step command delay in the evaluation code.

Though these measures trimmed flashy claims, they uncovered the paper's core insights: sample independence constraints, timing bugs, and the reversal of one-step metrics.

sections.heading: Ten practical rules for using learned simulators with legged robots
sections.summary: Synthesizing the experimental findings, this section outlines ten actionable guidelines for practitioners aiming to train legged robot controllers inside learned world models.
sections.details:
### 11.1 Why Do Accurate Simulators Yield Bad Policies?
Why does lower open-loop error lead to broken policies? The answer lies in the adversarial nature of reinforcement learning. Policy optimizers aggressively exploit simulator blind spots—unrealistic dynamics where the model inadvertently grants high reward. Without exposure to off-policy actions or fall recovery, even models with low prediction error on logged data get exploited.

### 11.2 Ten Practical Rules for Practitioners
1. **Train on self-rollouts**: Unrolling the model autoregressively for at least 8 steps is necessary to learn contracting, error-damping dynamics.
2. **Never select architectures using one-step error**: One-step evaluations favor teacher forcing and reverse long-term rankings.
3. **Evaluate at the policy's operating horizon** (100 steps or more).
4. **8-bit quantization is safe, but pruning requires fine-tuning**.
5. **Use uncertainty to rank, not as calibrated bounds**: Ensemble spread tracks relative risk well, but severely underestimates absolute variance.
6. **Scrutinize variance loss formulations**: Non-likelihood MSE formulations will inevitably drive variance predictions to zero.
7. **Never train simulators exclusively on successful runs**: Without fall data, simulators cannot model failure, enabling severe policy exploitation.
8. **Beware of fine-tuning on physics data**: As few as 20 iterations can strip a model's ability to support walking policies.
9. **Run a known policy inside the simulator**: Closed-loop tracking checks correlate far better with downstream success than open-loop error metrics.
10. **Count independent trajectories**: Never inflate statistical confidence with overlapping windows; compute significance across non-overlapping runs.

sections.heading: Limitations of this audit
sections.summary: The findings rely on a single robot (ANYmal D), a flat-ground trotting gait, and a hand-crafted MuJoCo model. No hardware experiments were conducted, and constraints from limited compute apply.
sections.details:
The authors explicitly outline the limitations of their audit:

- No Hardware Validation: All evaluations were performed on recorded datasets and a hand-built MuJoCo environment; real-world robot deployment was not tested.
- Narrow Operational Scope: Tests were restricted to flat-ground trotting across roughly 20 command velocities.
- Physics Engine Discrepancies: MuJoCo with an analytical actuator model was used as a surrogate rather than the original Isaac Lab setup with neural actuator networks.
- Limited Policy Training Budget: Compute constraints on the laptop limited reinforcement learning to 500 iterations, meaning the walking policies were not fully converged.
- Unknown Pre-training History: Detailed training logs for the public checkpoint (allegedly trained on 6M steps) were unavailable, leaving open the possibility that parts of the test data were in-sample for that model.

sections.heading: Conclusion: toward meaningful evaluation of world models
sections.summary: Deploying world models in robotics requires abandoning one-step accuracy in favor of closed-loop, policy-aware evaluation. This GPU-free audit offers a vital warning for robot learning research.
sections.details:
This study conducted an end-to-end audit of learned world models for legged robots. While confirming the necessity of self-rollout training as proposed by RWM, it provides definitive evidence against the widespread practice of ranking models via one-step prediction accuracy.

The discovery that fine-tuning a model to improve open-loop accuracy can simultaneously destroy its ability to support walking policies exposes the severe objective mismatch at the heart of learned simulation. Building effective simulators requires moving beyond offline prediction metrics toward system-level evaluations that probe how stably the model supports policy exploration.

Future work calls for standardizing closed-loop checks, compiling datasets that capture failure modes and falls, and testing on physical hardware. Begun on a modest everyday laptop, this audit demonstrates the immense value of reproducibility and healthy skepticism in the fast-moving field of robot learning.

takeaways: Never evaluate learned simulators using one-step prediction error; assessing whether errors compound or contract requires multi-step rollouts or Lyapunov exponent analysis.
High open-loop prediction accuracy does not guarantee walking policies; reinforcement learning exploits unmodeled dynamics, making closed-loop evaluation essential.
Ensemble uncertainty reliably ranks relative danger across states, but its absolute magnitude is severely overconfident, making raw values unsafe for use as calibrated error bars.
When compressing simulators, assess performance retention at the policy's operational horizon (e.g., 2 seconds) rather than one step ahead, using brief fine-tuning to recover lost skill.
limitations: Experiments are limited to a single task—flat-ground trotting on the ANYmal D quadruped—and have not been validated on rough terrain, other gaits, or different robot morphologies.
All policy trials were conducted within a hand-crafted MuJoCo simulation environment without physical robot hardware validation.
Due to compute constraints (a 2017 dual-core laptop), reinforcement learning was limited to 500 iterations, yielding partially trained walking controllers.
